messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 64

He is an 80-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his life in the Coast Guard, a career that gave shape to his identity long before he had words for what it cost him. He speaks of service with pride, and of discipline almost as a family inheritance. For decades, he trusted routines, weather reports, clear commands, and the sense that if he did everything correctly, people would come home alive. That belief is shattered by one event that still organizes his days.

Many years ago, while on duty, he accidentally causes serious injury to another person. He describes it not as a dramatic or heroic moment, but as a terrible mistake that happens in a sequence of ordinary actions. One decision leads to another, and then there is a sound, a cry, and an irreversible change in the room. In the immediate aftermath, he does what trained men do: he moves, reports, helps, follows procedure. But inside, he feels frozen. Even then, he knows something has split open in him. He later says that the injured person’s face seems to remain with him more vividly than any medal, promotion, or mission ever does.

In the years that follow, he returns to work because that is what he knows. He keeps his posture straight, his voice controlled, and his eyes on the task. Colleagues experience him as reliable, reserved, almost stoic. He does not talk about the event and does not allow himself much space for guilt. At home, his wife notices that he becomes quieter, more irritable, and increasingly restless at night. He wakes suddenly, sometimes reaching for something that is not there, and lies awake listening to the house settle around him. He starts checking locks, doors, and alarms repeatedly, as if vigilance might undo what has already happened. He avoids news stories, accident scenes, and any conversation that might turn toward responsibility or loss.

Over time, his life narrows around avoidance. He keeps busy with work and later with small household tasks, but there is always a strain in the effort. He does not like being in crowded places, especially if there is sudden noise or movement. A shout, a metal clang, or the sight of blood can jolt him so sharply that he feels his chest tighten and his mind go blank for a moment. He says he never fully knows when the memory will come; sometimes it arrives as a flash of image, sometimes as a bodily sense that he is back in that instant before the injury. When that happens, he becomes rigid and silent, then abruptly irritable if anyone asks what is wrong. He dislikes this part of himself most because anger feels, to him, dangerously close to the helplessness he carries.

His wife becomes the person who sees the cost of his silence. She learns to read his moods and gives him space when he withdraws. He is loving in practical ways, but emotionally distant. He struggles to accept comfort, and when she tries to reassure him that accidents happen, he feels a surge of shame he cannot bear to name. After she dies, his isolation deepens. Widowed and older, he has fewer distractions and more time with memory. The nights become especially difficult. He sleeps lightly, wakes often, and sometimes sits in the dark until morning, replaying the event as if a different outcome might still be found if he thinks hard enough.

Now, in his later years, the memory has not softened with age. Instead, it seems to have become more present as his world has grown quieter. He remains proud of his years in the Coast Guard, yet that pride is threaded through with self-condemnation. He speaks with care, often pausing before answering, as though he is choosing which parts of the story can be safely touched. He still tries to manage his days through habit and duty, but the old alertness is exhausted by the burden of guilt. There are moments when he sits alone and feels the full weight of having harmed someone by mistake, and in those moments he does not think of himself as an old man, only as the person he was at the instant everything went wrong.
